title: Energy and its forms
lede: Energy is never made or destroyed, only moved and changed. Follow it and you can explain a punch, a crash, a power bill and the food on your plate.

sections.md:
## What energy is
**Energy** is the ability to do **work**: to move something by pushing it through a distance. Both are measured in **joules (J)**.

**Work = force × distance** (with the force in the direction of motion)

Push a stalled car with 500 N for 10 m and you've done 500 × 10 = **5,000 J** of work, transferring 5,000 J of energy into the car. Push a wall all day and you do **zero** work on it (it doesn't move), even though you're exhausted. Your muscles burn energy internally, but none goes into the wall.

## Kinetic energy: energy of motion
**KE = ½ · m · v²**

Two things to notice:
- Double the **mass** → double the energy.
- Double the **speed** → **four times** the energy, because speed is squared.

That square is why speed matters so much in crashes and in fights. A punch's energy depends far more on hand speed than on arm mass. And all that kinetic energy has to go somewhere when a truck stops: into the brakes as **heat**. That's why brakes fade on long downhill grades: they overheat.

sections.title: Car vs truck at the same speed
sections.problem: Both go 25 m/s (about 56 mph). Car: 1,500 kg. Loaded truck: 36,000 kg.
sections.answer: The truck carries **24 times** the energy. Its brakes have to turn all of it into heat to stop.

sections.md:
## Potential energy: stored energy
Energy stored by position or condition:

- **Gravitational**: **PE = m · g · h**. Lift something higher and you store energy in it.
- **Elastic**: a stretched band, a compressed spring, a drawn bow.
- **Chemical**: stored in the bonds of fuel, food and batteries.
- **Nuclear**: stored in atomic nuclei; released in the Sun and in power plants.

## Conservation of energy
**Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves.** This is one of the most tested laws in all of science; no experiment has ever broken it.

A dropped rock: **PE at the top** → turns into **KE** on the way down → at impact, turns into **sound, heat and deformation**. The total never changes.

So where does energy go when things "lose" it? Almost always into **thermal energy**: random motion of molecules, i.e., heat. It's still there. It's just spread out and hard to use again.

sections.q: A roller coaster car (no friction) starts at rest at the top of a 45 m hill. At the bottom, its kinetic energy equals…
options: its potential energy at the top
half its potential energy at the top
twice its potential energy at the top
sections.why: With no friction, **all** the PE becomes KE. Energy is conserved.

sections.title: Speed from height
sections.problem: A wrench falls off a 20 m bridge. How fast is it going when it hits the water? (Ignore air.)
steps: PE at top = KE at bottom: m·g·h = ½·m·v².
sections.answer: **About 19.8 m/s** (≈ 44 mph). Notice the mass canceled: a wrench and a bolt hit at the same speed.

sections.md:
## Power: how fast energy moves
**Power = energy ÷ time**, measured in **watts (W)**. 1 W = 1 J per second.

- **1 horsepower ≈ 746 W.** A 500 hp truck engine can deliver about 373,000 J every second.
- Your power bill charges by the **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: 1,000 W running for 1 hour = **3.6 million J**.

Two people can do the same **work** climbing a flight of stairs; the one who sprints up uses more **power**.

## Food is energy too
A food **Calorie** (capital C) is a kilocalorie: **1 Calorie = 4,184 J**.

A 3,100-Calorie day is about **13 million joules**, roughly the kinetic energy of that loaded truck at highway speed. When you train, your muscles turn only about 20–25% of the energy they burn into motion; the rest becomes body heat. That's why you get hot when you train.

## Efficiency
**Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in.**

No machine is 100% efficient; some energy always ends up as heat. Rough numbers:

| Machine | Efficiency |
|---|---|
| Gasoline car engine | about 20–35% |
| Big diesel truck engine | about 40–45% at its best |
| Electric motor | about 85–95% |
| LED bulb (energy → light) | far better than old incandescent bulbs (~5%) |

So when you fill up a gas car, most of the fuel's energy heats the engine and the air.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Work needs motion in the direction of the force.** Carrying a box across a level room does almost no work on the box, physics-wise, because you push up and it moves sideways.
- **"Using up" energy** really means turning it into less useful forms, mostly heat.
- **KE grows with v², not v.** Most people underestimate how much more dangerous 80 mph is than 60 mph: (80/60)² ≈ 1.78, so about 78% more energy.

practice.q: You push a crate with 300 N for 4 m. Work done?
Kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s?
Potential energy of a 10 kg box on a 5 m shelf? (g = 9.8)
If you double a car's speed, its kinetic energy becomes…
Where does most of a truck's kinetic energy go when it brakes to a stop?
practice.why: Friction in the brakes turns KE into **thermal energy**.

practice.q: A 1,200 W microwave runs for 30 seconds. Energy used?
A machine takes in 1,000 J and puts out 250 J of useful work. Its efficiency is…
You hold a 20 kg barbell overhead, perfectly still, for 30 seconds. Work done **on the barbell**:
practice.why: It doesn't move, so **no work** is done on it. Your muscles still burn energy internally.

practice.q: A stone falls from rest off a 45 m cliff. Speed at the bottom? (g = 9.8, ignore air; round to 1 decimal)
practice.hint: Set PE at the top equal to KE at the bottom. The mass cancels.

practice.q: A 1,500 W space heater runs 4 hours a day for 30 days at $0.15 per kWh. Cost in dollars?
practice.hint: Convert watts to kilowatts, multiply by hours, then by the price.

practice.q: A truck goes from 60 mph to 80 mph. Its kinetic energy goes up by about…
practice.why: KE ∝ v². (80 ÷ 60)² = (4/3)² = 16/9 ≈ 1.78, so about **78% more** energy, and about 78% more braking distance.
practice.hint: Square the ratio of the speeds.

practice.q: A 3,100-Calorie day of food is how many **million** joules? (1 Calorie = 4,184 J; round to 1 decimal)
